strengths: Tackles a highly timely and important problem: correcting bias and constructing valid confidence intervals for the widely used LLM-as-a-judge evaluation paradigm.

The statistical framework is theoretically rigorous, adapting classical misclassification corrections (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014) to provide a principled treatment of both test-set and calibration-set uncertainty.
Introduces a highly practical, adaptive calibration sample allocation strategy (Algorithm 1) that minimizes confidence interval length under a fixed budget.
Provides valuable, rigorous insights showing when LLM-as-a-judge with calibration is statistically more efficient (lower variance) than direct human evaluation.
Exhibits strong robustness to label distribution shifts between calibration and test sets, outperforming alternative approaches like standard Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) under such shifts.
Well-written with clear explanations, illustrative figures, thorough simulation studies, and a realistic evaluation on Chatbot Arena.
weaknesses: The statistical novelty is somewhat limited, as the core point estimator and confidence interval are direct applications of existing statistical literature (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014).

The framework is primarily developed for binary evaluation (correct/incorrect). While binary setup covers many scenarios, many common LLM benchmarks rely on multi-class, Likert-scale (1-10), or pairwise with ties (win/loss/tie) setups, which are only briefly mentioned as future work.

The assumption of invariant sensitivity and specificity ($Pr_P(\hat{Z} \mid Z) = Pr_Q(\hat{Z} \mid Z)$) may violate under covariate shifts (e.g., if the test set contains much harder or longer responses than the calibration set), which could introduce residual bias.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and widespread issue in LLM evaluation: the presence of systematic bias and the lack of robust uncertainty quantification (confidence intervals) in the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm.

Provides a statistically rigorous foundation by adapting classical epidemiological and measurement error correction methods (Rogan & Gladen, Lang & Reiczigel) to the LLM-as-a-judge framework, accounting for both test-set and calibration-set variance.

Introduces a novel adaptive allocation strategy (Algorithm 1) to optimize the human labeling budget for the calibration dataset, which is shown both theoretically and empirically to minimize confidence interval length.

Demonstrates robust performance under label distribution shifts. The theoretical comparison of various estimators under distribution shift (Table 1, Figure 5) is highly illuminating, proving that the proposed estimator is uniquely robust when the marginal label distributions differ.

The paper is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality illustrations (such as Figures 2, 4, and 5) that make complex statistical concepts easily accessible. A plug-and-play Python implementation is also provided in the appendix, enhancing usability and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The current framework is restricted to binary outcomes (e.g., correct/incorrect, binary preference). While many evaluations fit this paradigm, many others utilize Likert scales (1-5) or multinomial classification, which are not handled by the current formulation.

The assumption of an invariant confusion matrix ($Pr(\hat{Z} | Z)$) across the calibration and test sets may be violated if the difficulty or composition of the queries changes significantly. Although the authors acknowledge this limitation in Section 9 (Future Work), the current paper lacks an empirical sensitivity analysis exploring how minor violations of this assumption affect the estimator's bias and coverage.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and timely problem: correcting the inherent bias of LLM-as-a-judge evaluators and providing mathematically sound confidence intervals.
The theoretical foundation is robust, building on and extending classical statistical literature (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014) to the LLM evaluation paradigm.
The adaptive allocation strategy (Proposition 5.2 and Algorithm 1) is highly practical, showing how to optimize a human annotation budget to minimize the confidence interval length.

The analysis in Section 6 is highly insightful, demonstrating mathematically when calibrated LLM evaluation is more sample-efficient (lower variance) than fully human evaluation for a fixed labeling budget.

The discussion on distribution shift (Section 7) is excellent, clearly showing why the proposed misclassification-adjusted estimator is more robust to label shift than existing methods like standard PPI.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality figures, comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations, realistic Chatbot Arena experiments, and clean, self-contained Python code.
weaknesses: The core assumption that the confusion matrix (sensitivity q1 and specificity q0) is invariant across datasets (i.e., Pr_P(Z_hat | Z) = Pr_Q(Z_hat | Z)) may not always hold. In practice, the difficulty of instances or covariate features (e.g., prompt topic, response length) can affect the judge's error rate. The paper would be strengthened by an empirical investigation into how sensitive the estimator is to violations of this assumption.

The current framework is restricted to binary judgments. While the authors discuss multinomial extensions in future work, many LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks rely on multi-class rankings (e.g., win/loss/tie) or multi-point Likert scales, limiting the immediate applicability of the exact formulas presented here.

It is unclear how ties were handled in the Chatbot Arena experiments (Section 8.2), as standard Chatbot Arena votes and LLM evaluations often include ties, whereas the proposed method is strictly binary.

strengths: Addresses a critical and highly timely issue in LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, where naive accuracy scores are widely reported without adjusting for judge bias or establishing confidence intervals.

The statistical foundation is robust, effectively reintroducing classical epidemiological and survey statistics techniques (Rogan-Gladen adjustment) to the modern machine learning evaluation pipeline.

The paper offers a valuable and rigorous comparison between LLM-based evaluation and human-only evaluation (Section 6), identifying the exact parameter regimes where using an adjusted LLM-as-a-judge is statistically more efficient than human-only evaluation.

Crucially demonstrates that the proposed estimator remains unbiased under distribution shifts in the target accuracy ($Pr_P(Z) \neq Pr_Q(Z)$). The analysis in Section 8 elegantly exposes how other popular methods like Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) can introduce bias under such shifts.
Provides a highly practical, adaptive calibration allocation strategy (Algorithm 1) that helps practitioners minimize the length of confidence intervals under a fixed annotation budget.
The presentation is outstanding, featuring intuitive figures, clear mathematical derivations, and a clean Python implementation that ensures high reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core point estimator and adjusted Wald interval are directly adapted from classic statistics literature (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014), meaning the fundamental statistical novelty is somewhat limited.

The framework is currently restricted to binary outcomes (correct/incorrect or win/loss). Extending this to multi-class settings, Likert scales, or pairwise comparison with ties is mentioned in the future work section but not fully developed or empirically validated.

The conditional invariance assumption ($Pr_P(\hat{Z}|Z) = Pr_Q(\hat{Z}|Z)$) might be violated if other latent covariates (such as prompt difficulty or response length) shift significantly between the calibration and test sets, which could affect the LLM's sensitivity and specificity in practice.

strengths: The paper is exceptionally well-written, clear, and logically structured.
Provides a highly practical and mathematically sound solution to a major current issue in the LLM literature: the statistical bias of LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.

The analysis of distribution shift (Section 8) is a major strength. It elegantly demonstrates why standard prediction-powered inference (PPI) and other calibration estimators can become biased under label/accuracy shifts, whereas the misclassification-adjusted estimator (Rogan & Gladen, 1978) remains robust because it only assumes the invariance of the judge's conditional error rates.
Introduces an innovative adaptive allocation strategy (Algorithm 1) to optimize human annotation budgets for calibration, which yields tighter confidence intervals.
Provides a thorough comparison against human-only evaluation, defining the exact parameter regimes where LLM-as-a-judge is statistically more efficient.
weaknesses: The core estimator and its confidence intervals are directly adopted from existing statistical literature (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014), limiting the novelty of the fundamental statistical framework.

The invariance assumption on the judge's conditional behavior $P(\hat{Z} | Z)$ may be violated if the distribution shift involves changes in the 'difficulty' or 'ambiguity' of the test items, which could cause the sensitivity and specificity to shift. A brief empirical investigation or sensitivity analysis on this potential limitation would strengthen the work.

The framework is currently restricted to binary outcomes. While applicable to pairwise win-rates (such as Chatbot Arena), many LLM evaluations utilize multi-class/Likert-scale (1-5) scoring, which is left as future work.

strengths: Timely and important topic: addressing bias and uncertainty in LLM-as-a-judge evaluations is highly relevant as these evaluations are widely used but often lack statistical rigor.

Insightful analysis of distribution shift: the paper clearly demonstrates why the misclassification-adjusted estimator (Rogan-Gladen style) remains unbiased under shifts in the target label distribution Pr(Z), while popular alternatives like Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) can become biased.
Exceptional clarity and presentation: the paper is very well-written, featuring intuitive explanations, clear figures, and a complete Python implementation in the appendix.
Solid theoretical and empirical validation: the theoretical results are mathematically sound and backed by thorough simulations as well as real-world evaluations on Chatbot Arena.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core estimator and confidence intervals are direct applications of classic statistical methods from Rogan & Gladen (1978) and Lang & Reiczigel (2014) respectively.

Practical bottleneck of the adaptive allocation strategy: Algorithm 1 requires collecting a specific number of calibration samples of each true label class (m0 and m1). However, since true labels are unknown prior to human annotation, it is unclear how one can selectively allocate these samples without over-annotating and discarding data, which would undermine the fixed-budget advantage.

Strong invariance assumption: the robustness under distribution shift assumes that the LLM judge's sensitivity and specificity Pr(Z_hat | Z) remain perfectly constant. In practice, shifts in the complexity or style of responses within each class could easily alter these parameters, potentially re-introducing bias.

strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and timely problem: correcting bias and establishing statistically sound confidence intervals for LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.
The paper is very well-written, with clear explanations, helpful illustrations, and a practical, easy-to-use Python implementation.
Proposes an adaptive calibration data allocation strategy (Algorithm 1) that optimizes sample sizes to minimize the confidence interval length under a budget.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core point estimator and confidence interval formulation are direct applications of classical epidemiological prevalence estimation techniques (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014).

Lack of real-world evaluation: the empirical validation is conducted entirely on synthetic Monte Carlo simulations. The paper lacks validation on actual LLM-as-a-judge evaluation datasets with human ground-truth labels.

Strong simplifying assumptions: the model assumes constant specificity ($q_0$) and sensitivity ($q_1$) across all evaluation instances, which likely fails in practice where LLM judgment errors depend heavily on instance difficulty.
Lack of comparative analysis with modern alternatives such as Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI), which also provides unbiased estimates and valid confidence intervals under weaker assumptions.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and timely topic: the statistical validity of LLM-as-a-judge evaluations, which are widely used but often suffer from bias and unquantified uncertainty.

Excellent presentation and clarity. The explanation of the bias under imperfect specificity/sensitivity and the dual sources of uncertainty (test set vs. calibration set) is intuitive and mathematically rigorous.

The introduction of the adaptive calibration sample allocation (Algorithm 1 and Proposition 2) is a very practical and elegant contribution to minimize confidence interval lengths under a fixed human labeling budget.
The code is clearly documented and provided directly in the paper, making the proposed method highly reproducible and easy to adopt.
weaknesses: The core statistical framework for bias correction and confidence interval construction is directly imported from existing work in prevalence estimation (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014), which limits the technical novelty of the statistical methodology.

The empirical validation is conducted entirely via synthetic Monte Carlo simulations. The paper would be significantly stronger if it evaluated the method on real-world datasets with real LLM judges (e.g., MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, or GSM8K) and compared the calibrated results against actual human annotations.

The assumption of constant sensitivity ($q_1$) and specificity ($q_0$) across the calibration and test sets is crucial but highly fragile in practice. Real-world evaluations often suffer from covariate shift (e.g., the test set distribution of difficulty or topics differs from the calibration set), which could violate this assumption and lead to miscalibrated intervals. The paper lacks a discussion or sensitivity analysis on this potential issue.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly relevant and timely problem: the statistical biases and unquantified uncertainty in LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.
The writing is exceptionally clear, logical, and easy to follow. The figures and diagrams (such as Figures 1 and 2) are highly intuitive and clarify the concepts well.
The proposed adaptive allocation algorithm (Algorithm 1) is a practical, statistically justified, and novel way to minimize confidence interval lengths under a fixed calibration budget.
The paper promotes good scientific practices by providing clean, self-contained Python code in the appendix, making the method immediately applicable for practitioners.
weaknesses: The core statistical framework (the bias-corrected point estimator and the adjusted Wald confidence interval) is largely a direct application of classical work from epidemiology/prevalence estimation (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014), which limits the theoretical novelty.

The empirical validation is conducted entirely via synthetic Monte Carlo simulations. The paper would be significantly stronger if the method were evaluated on real-world LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks (e.g., MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, or factual consistency datasets) using actual human-annotated ground-truth calibration data.

The framework assumes constant sensitivity ($q_1$) and specificity ($q_0$) across all instances. In practice, LLM evaluator accuracy can vary significantly depending on the difficulty, domain, or length of the specific response being evaluated, which may violate the assumed simple binomial error model.

strengths: Addresses a timely, highly relevant, and practical problem in machine learning: the statistical bias and lack of uncertainty quantification in LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.

Brings classical, robust statistical techniques (Rogan & Gladen's misclassification adjustment and the adjusted Wald confidence interval) into the LLM evaluation era, providing a clean and easily implementable framework.

Provides an insightful theoretical and empirical analysis of distribution shift, showing that while popular methods like Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) can become biased when the proportion of positive labels shifts, the proposed sensitivity/specificity-based correction remains unbiased.
Proposes a practical adaptive allocation strategy (Algorithm 1) to distribute calibration samples between classes, successfully minimizing the resulting confidence interval length.
Validated through rigorous Monte Carlo simulations and extensive real-world experiments on Chatbot Arena and AlpacaEval across multiple state-of-the-art LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, Gemini).
weaknesses: The core statistical formulation relies heavily on established methods (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014), meaning the fundamental methodological novelty is somewhat modest.

The assumption that the judge's sensitivity and specificity remain perfectly invariant (Pr_P(Z_hat | Z) = Pr_Q(Z_hat | Z)) under distribution shift may be violated in practice if the shift is driven by latent covariates (e.g., task difficulty or response style) that degrade the judge's accuracy.

Scaling the method to multi-category grading (as shown in Appendix B) or continuous scores faces the curse of dimensionality, as estimating a large k x k confusion matrix requires a much larger human-labeled calibration dataset.

strengths: Highly relevant and timely work addressing a major flaw in current LLM-as-a-judge evaluation methodologies, namely the lack of statistical calibration and confidence intervals.
Excellent clarity in presentation, with outstanding figures and a very clear educational tone that makes the statistical concepts accessible to LLM practitioners.
Rigorous statistical analysis, including a formal characterization of when LLM-as-a-judge is statistically more efficient than human-only evaluation (Proposition 6.1).

Clear demonstration of why this Rogan-Gladen-style estimator is superior to prediction-powered inference (PPI) under target distribution shift, which is a highly common scenario in benchmark evaluation.
The proposed adaptive calibration allocation strategy is practical and effectively minimizes the confidence interval width under a fixed budget.
weaknesses: The core statistical framework (estimator and confidence interval derivation) relies heavily on existing literature (Rogan & Gladen, 1978; Lang & Reiczigel, 2014).

The assumption that conditional LLM error rates $Pr(\hat{Z} | Z)$ remain invariant under distribution shift may be violated if the difficulty of the test instances changes, which could limit the estimator's robustness in practice.
The multi-category extension requires estimating a $k \times k$ confusion matrix, which scales poorly and may require a significantly larger calibration set when some categories are rare.

strengths: Highly relevant and timely topic: LLM-as-a-judge is widely used in the ML community, but naive accuracy reporting is biased and lacks proper uncertainty quantification. This paper provides a principled, statistically sound correction.

Comprehensive analysis of distribution shift: Showing that the proposed estimator (Rogan-Gladen) remains unbiased when the test set accuracy differs from the calibration set accuracy, whereas other popular methods like Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI) can become biased under such shifts, is a highly valuable insight for the community.
Practical contributions: The adaptive allocation strategy (Algorithm 1) for optimizing calibration sample size allocation under a fixed budget is very useful for practitioners.
Excellent presentation and clarity: The paper is exceptionally well-written, with clear figures (especially Figures 2, 6, and 8) that intuitively convey the core ideas and empirical findings.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The core point estimator (Rogan & Gladen, 1978) and confidence interval (Lang & Reiczigel, 2014) are established statistical methods. The primary novelty lies in their application to LLM evaluation, the characterization of the favorable parameter regimes, and the adaptive allocation strategy.

Sensitivity to covariate shift: The assumption that the LLM judge's sensitivity and specificity are invariant between the calibration and test sets ($Pr_P(\hat{Z}|Z) = Pr_Q(\hat{Z}|Z)$) may be violated in practice if the test set has different prompt characteristics (e.g., length, style, difficulty). While acknowledged in the limitations, the paper does not quantitatively analyze the estimator's sensitivity to mild violations of this assumption.

Sample complexity in multi-class settings: The multi-class extension in Appendix B requires estimating a $k \times k$ confusion matrix, which significantly increases the required calibration size. More analysis on how to handle sample-starved categories in this setup would make the extension more practically viable.
